 Best business laptops: FAQs 
 What are the best laptops for business? 
 It will depend on what sort of business tasks you're undertaking, but generally, the best Dell laptops and the best ThinkPad laptops are ideal for Windows users, while we've also reviewed the best business MacBooks and best MacBook Pro laptops for those who prefer macOS. These laptops for business users are tailored for work and are, in our experience, fast, robust, and reliable. All critical for those looking to boost productivity. 
 We've also found some - but not all - the best HP laptops are great if you're working to a budget, and many at the lower end of the range are absolutely perfect for running Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and general web browsing. Lenovo has been making an impressive push recently too. 
 What features should I look for in a business laptop?
 We asked Zach Noskey, Director of Portfolio Vision & Strategy at Dell Technologies, what he thought
 There are many important features that differentiate a business laptop from a traditional consumer laptop. Specific capabilities to consider when purchasing a fleet of PCs will depend on the type of business and the role and responsibilities of employees, but below are a few broad areas to prioritize:
 Collaboration : With the growth of hybrid work, employees need the capabilities to collaborate and connect from anywhere. Business workers rely on best-in-class video and audio features for frequent conference calls. Look for a minimum FHD camera for quality picture, top firing speakers for improved sound, and Wi-Fi 6E and 5G for a variety of connectivity options.
 Design : Workers need mobile and flexible form factors for working on-the-go. Business laptops should ideally be lightweight and small, but also include a 16:10 aspect ratio display for an optimal front of screen experience. Plus, they should be made with durable and premium materials built to last.
 Performance : Performance is a given for maximum productivity. Choose business laptops equipped with the latest generation of processors available to run applications smoothly when multi-tasking and preserve battery life. CPU and GPU specifics, such as discrete graphics, will depend on the demands of a worker’s role. Finally, look for systems with a minimum of 16GB of dual-channel memory and at least 512GB of SSD drive space.
 Security and support: It’s not only about the end user experience. IT departments need enterprise-level hardware/firmware and software security features to prevent, detect and respond to threats wherever they occur. Plus, IT needs reliable service and support options for their fleet of PCs. Depending on the size of the business, companies might consider an all-in-one IT support option that handles all elements of hardware management, or choose a flexible offering that helps simplify deploying the latest PCs.
 What are the key differences between the best business laptops and laptops for home?
 We asked Eric Ackerson, Senior Product Marketing & Brand Manager, Acer America
 There are significant design and hardware differences between consumer and business laptops. In most cases, business models are made with more durable materials and construction to withstand the rigors of travel and toting the laptop to and from the office. This means they’re typically built with more metal in the chassis as compared to plastic that’s often used in consumer models. Many are MIL-STD 810H-certified with spill-resistant keyboards and touchpads to protect internal components from liquids. Shock-resistant features and semi-ruggedized designs help protect them from short drops. Business laptops focus on durability, reliability, performance and life span, which often means a long battery life and the ability to upgrade the laptop over time. Consumer laptops have more focus on style and value for today’s computing needs.
 Another key difference is in the software installed on the systems. Business laptops will come with Windows 11 Pro vs. Windows 11 Home. Windows 11 Pro has many features supporting business management and deployment, which aren’t necessary for consumer computers. These laptops will typically have other manageability features built-in to aid IT departments in diagnosing, updating systems remotely and deploying to their workforce. In contrast, consumer laptops are often loaded with entertainment-focused applications for social media, gaming and digital hobbies that business workers do not need and IT departments may see as security risks. Simplifying the software pre-load for large quantities of business laptops purchased in bulk eases setup, deployment and management of these laptops.
 In addition, Windows 11 Pro provides extra security features through hardware-based security, such as TPM 2.0, virtualization-based security (VBM) and hypervisor protected code integrity (HVCI). Software-based security adds advanced encryption, robust network and system security and intelligent safeguards, which improve over time against ever-evolving threats. Laptops designed for business may also come with sensors that detect people based on range and movement. These laptops can lock the screen when the user steps away and also blur the screen to off-angle viewing to prevent someone seeing the screen’s content over a user’s shoulder.
 Another factor differentiating business models is the warranty. Consumer laptops typically have a one-year warranty, while commercial warranties may last up to three years and cover on-site service from a technician and the provision of spare parts.
 Finally, business laptops are more conservative in style and color in comparison to consumer versions, to keep a low profile and blend in commercial settings. Consumer models, particularly those designed for gaming, may come in bright colors and with multi-colored RGB keyboards.
 In conclusion, there are significant differences between consumer and business laptops. While each type of laptop serves its purpose, it is important to consider needs and priorities before making a purchase. Whether you are looking for advanced security features or budget-friendly options, there is a laptop on the market to meet your needs.
 How to choose the best business laptops 
 Finding the best laptop for you is all about deciding what you consider most important and focusing on those needs before considering other requirements. If you work in an office, battery life might not be critical, but it might be vital for those working away from a desk.
 Laptop makers offer many devices, each aimed at a specific user and usage profile. Therefore it's essential to consider the role this system will play in the office and what it needs to support that. You should also check if your company has a preferred operating system. Both Windows and macOS are ideal for most work settings.
 Here are some of the aspects that we consider the most important.
 Specs & performance 
 The performance available from a modern laptop can be awe-inspiring. Many more expensive models have potent processors, NVMe storage, and discrete GPUs - and if you're a creative professional, you'll want to see our guides to the best laptops for photo editing and the best laptops for video editing .
 Typically, cheap machines come with an Intel Celeron or Core i3 class processor, and they're only suitable for relatively light office tasks. Above them are devices that use the Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5, and these are the workhorses that can cope with most tasks by having lots of processing cores and multi-threaded processors. And on the top rung are the Intel Core-7 and Core-i9 mobile processors and the AMD Ryzen 7 class CPUs. These powerhouse systems can be used for very intensive tasks often allocated to desktop computers, and they can come with discrete GPU technology.
 For integrated GPUs, the lesser machines have the old Intel UHD Graphics module, and in newer Intel chips, this has been supplanted by the Iris Xe GPU. Conversely, AMD systems have either the older Radeon Graphics or, the better Radeon 680M.
 The discrete GPU options are usually based around either Nvidia RTX or AMD RX technology, with various performance tiers available. What's important to understand is that mobile GPUs aren't comparable to desktop equivalents. Therefore, don't expect an Nvidia RTX 3060 mobile GPU to perform like that same designation in a PCIe card for a desktop system.
 Because of power limitations and heat generation, mobile GPUs tend to be cut down from the desktop regarding shaders, memory buses, and clock speeds.
 Battery Life 
 The extent of battery life depends on several factors, not least the battery capacity and how efficiently the system uses the stored power.
 While having a bigger battery is suitable for how long it will last without mains power, it tends to increase the machine's weight, and depending on the charger, it can take longer to recharge.
 One of the downsides of more powerful processors is that they will consume more power, and the same is true for discrete GPUs over integrated, high-performance NVMe drives and exceptionally bright displays.
 How this translates into the working life of batteries isn't easy to calculate. Still, the difference between a machine using power-saving mode with reduced screen brightness and another using performance settings with an intensive task can be substantial.
 The better machines running standard office tasks or playing YouTube videos can last longer than ten hours, and the worst under four.
 It is worth pointing out that the newest technology, i.e., Intel 13th Gen and AMD Ryzen 7000 processors, are much more power efficient than previous technologies. Older tech might be cheaper, but it won't last as long on battery, doing the same jobs as something with more modern silicon, as a rule.
 Connectivity 
 Having plenty of port selection is critical if you're hooking up a lot of different devices, from the best business monitors to the best office keyboards . However, This aspect is essential for those considering any of the best Ultrabooks and 2-in-1 designs especially often have limited external ports.
 The solution to the limited port selection is to use a docking station. The very best laptop docking stations provide both port extensions and simultaneously charge a business laptop - ideal when working on-the-go.
 In our experience, Thunderbolt is best, but the laptop must have at least one of these versatile ports to connect both power and data over a single connection. Achieving similar functionality over USB 3.2 Gen 2 USB-C is possible, but the bandwidth is less. That reduction impacts the flexibility, as the number of peripherals it can handle and the number of downstream ports is less.
 If you can afford a machine with a Thunderbolt port(s) and a Thunderbolt docking station, then whatever other ports are on that laptop are largely unimportant.
 One point about docking stations: they are usually rated for the watts they can deliver to an attached laptop, i.e., 65W or 83W. Some of the larger mobile workstation designs can draw up to 100W or more, and while these will charge on a docking station that can deliver 65W, it will take longer to charge fully.
 Network connections are often Wi-Fi, but some machines have an Ethernet adapter. However, if you have USB 3.2, a USB-to-Ethernet adapter is an inexpensive but valuable accessory.
 As for Wi-Fi, some cheaper machines have Wi-Fi 5, but the better ones have Wi-Fi 6 or 6E. If you intend to connect over Wi-Fi, it might be helpful to know the Wi-Fi routers' technology and a specific system design to work best with them.
 Survivability 
 It might seem an obvious thing to mention, but laptops get broken every day. They fail due to a manufacturing mistake, the owner being clumsy, unexpected vehicle accidents, and flood damage. The number of ways they can cease to be useful is a remarkably long list.
 Cheaper machines tend to use an aluminum frame with plastic panels attached that aren't best suited to survive a drop or being doused with hot coffee, not least being outside in the rain. Higher-end machines tend to use more metal, making them intrinsically more likely to handle some abuse.
 But, if you intend to work outdoors, in a wet or dusty environment, or have the skill of a lucky dip machine, then the best rugged laptops offer a robust and sturdy alternative. No machine is beyond being damaged by the creative things people do with them, but some are better suited to brush off accidents that would kill cheaper systems instantly.
 How we test the best business laptops 
 Why you can trust TechRadar
 ✅ More than 1,800 laptops, Chromebooks, and MacBooks reviewed
✅ Over 15 years of product testing
✅ Over 16,000 products reviewed in total
✅ Nearly 200,000 hours testing tech
 We've tested over 18000 laptops, MacBooks, and Chromebooks suitable for work, including the best laptops for working from home , the best laptops for work and gaming , and the best laptops for teachers working in education.
 Before we get to benchmarks and real-world testing, when reviewing the best business laptops we go through a familiarisation protocol. This is where we’ll use the machine for a few days for general tasks to establish if it is all working as intended and highlight any potential issues that the designers overlooked.
 During this phase, we’ve seen many problems, like hinges that cover up ports or trackpads unsuitable for adult-sized hands. Those issues are less common since many designs are derivatives of previous models with new motherboards rather than entirely new hardware.
 After testing the trackpad and keyboard, we usually remove the back of the machine to see inside the case unless we know a sticker is denying us access to the inside. In that scenario, it is usually possible to get a manual that reveals what we’d see, and that is crucial for us to determine if the laptop can be user upgraded, stickers or not.
 Many of the thinner Ultrabook and 2-in-1 models are now surface mounting memory, stopping that from being upgraded by the owner. But even those tend to have an M.2 slot for the NVMe drive that allows larger enterprises to be used. For those that have run the same system for many years, it might also be helpful to see what the spec of the battery pack is for that to be potentially replaced when it becomes worn out.
 After we’ve done that investigation and put the machine back in one piece, we begin our testing protocol, where we go through a selection of benchmarks that test different aspects of the hardware. These benchmarks include many synthetic tests like 3DMark, PCMark10, GeekBench, CineBench23, CPU-Z, CrystalDiskMark 8.04, and other real-world tools.
 These give a good oversight on single and multi-core processing, GPU performance, NVMe speed, and battery life.
 The battery test is part of PCMark10 that requires the screen to be dimmed to 120 nits and the performance setting of the machine put into a power-saving mode (but with the screen always active). The screen brightness is confirmed with the DataColor calibrator, and the test runs until the battery from total hits 20% of its capacity. From this test, it is possible to provide a ballpark time for how long a laptop will last without mains power.
 Exactly how it performs will depend on how it is used and how demanding those tasks are. Still, the calculated time should reveal if a fully working day on battery power is possible.
 All this data is then cross-checked with that collected from other testing sessions to establish where the machine fits into our bigger picture, specifically against other hardware that uses the same processor platform or against a previous model in the same series.

results.title: Acer Googlebook 14 review | IT Pro
results.text:
Acer Googlebook 14 review | IT Pro 
 (Image credit: Future)
IT Pro Verdict
Reasons to buy
 + Light, tough and flexible design
 + Excellent OLED screen
 + AI and smartphone features are impressive
 + Good mainstream performance
Reasons to avoid
 - Still needs more productivity and creative apps
 - Battery life is mediocre
By
 Stuart Andrews 
Published
30 October 2026
In
 Reviews 
 The Acer Googlebook 14 is the most accessible and affordable of the five Googlebooks in the initial launch line-up, bringing you a premium 14in convertible with prices starting at £999 inc VAT. Both the price and the laptop itself indicate how Googlebooks depart from existing Chromebook Plus devices. This isn't in any way a cut-price laptop. Google's Googlebook OS is new and somewhat idiosyncratic, but it's more ambitious and less compromised than Chrome OS has been in many areas. From its aluminium-magnesium chassis to its OLED screen to its Core Ultra 5 and Ultra 7 CPUs, the Googlebook 14 is designed to deliver a high-end experience akin to what you'd expect from a Pixel phone. It's informed by Google's experience with Chromebooks, but not constrained by it in the way that Google's Chromebook Plus devices were.
 It's undeniably a fascinating laptop, but can it handle serious professional use? Having spent a week working on the Googlebook 14, the answer is, well, complicated.

 Acer Googlebook 14: Design
 Acer hasn't completely developed its Googlebook from scratch, which makes perfect sense. It's been churning out excellent 13in and 14in 2-in-1 laptops for over a decade, and it's not hard to see echoes of previous Chromebook Plus Spin and Swift Spin devices in the Googlebook 14. It's a lightweight 2-in-1 convertible, 1.15Kg in weight and just under 14mm thick, with a tough magnesium-aluminium body. The familiar hinge allows the screen to unfold flat against the desktop or clamp against the base in a tablet configuration, or sit with the screen outwards in a tent configuration in-between. The latter setup can be useful for entertainment purposes or for ad-hoc presentations.
 Best picks for you
 Best business laptops 2026 
 Best Chromebooks 2026 
 Best business tablets 
 The inky dark blue finish gives it a very polished, professional styling, and Acer has cleverly kept the branding minimal, and even placed the signature Googlebook glowbar discreetly in the top-left corner of the lid. This shows a colour spectrum while the Googlebook is starting, then glows dimly while it's on as a subtle battery indicator. It also changes colour while Google's Gemini AI is active, to give you some visual feedback, though of course you won't actually see it given its positioning behind the screen. That's a sign that it's more about giving Googlebooks a shared visual identity than anything really practical.
 Latest Videos From IT Pro 
 Watch full video here: 
 Connectivity is equally stripped-back, with just three USB-C ports and a 3.5mm audio jack. Two of the USB-C ports are 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports, while the third is a Thunderbolt 4/USB 4.0 port, with data transfer speeds of up to 40Gbps. There's no dedicated HDMI or DisplayPort output, but you have DisplayPort 1.4 through the slower USB-C ports and DisplayPort 2.1 through the Thunderbolt 4 port. Meanwhile, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support mean you're up to date on wireless connectivity.
 The keyboard stretches across most of the laptop's deck, flanked by two slim top-firing DTS-branded speakers. There's a slightly odd, squishy feel to it at first, but also a few millimetres of travel and a nice, crisp tactile response. In practice, it's easy to get used to and very speedy, while Google has improved on the slightly odd Chromebook layout by retaining a Delete key in the top-right corner – next to the fingerprint and power button – and by allowing what's traditionally the Caps Lock to operate as both a Caps Lock and the more Google-specific Quick Insert key. As on Chromebooks, Quick Insert is handy for accessing AI features, but sometimes you just want a simple Caps Lock. Press Fn + Caps Lock and you have one.
 Meanwhile, Acer has fitted an enormous touchpad for a relatively compact laptop, spanning 125mm horizontally and 90mm vertically. It's silky smooth, sensitive, and very good at spotting gestures, which is handy as Googlebook OS gives us some new gestures to master. More on this later.
 Get the ITPro daily newsletter
 Sign up today and you will receive a free copy of our Future Focus 2026 report - the leading resource for IT decision-maker insight on priorities and investment areas in AI, security and more.
 Acer Googlebook 14: Display and features
 Acer has brought its A-game to its first Googlebook display, fitting a 14in 2880 x 1800 resolution OLED touchscreen with a 120Hz refresh rate. It's a beauty, especially with the Boosted color setting, giving you superb contrast, deep blacks, and extremely vibrant colors. It reaches a 541cd/m2 maximum brightness level with the Natural color setting and 609.4cd/m2 in Boosted, and it covers 100% of the sRGB color gamut with a 130% gamut volume. We couldn't replicate Acer's claimed 100% DCI-P3 coverage, but 91% isn't far off, and it also covers 89.6% of Adobe RGB. Color accuracy is solid, with an average Delta-E of just over 2.
 (Image credit: Future)
 We're not at the stage where many people will be doing color-critical design work on a Googlebook, but this screen wouldn't be an impediment if you needed to. The size and resolution also makes it a great workspace for running multiple productivity apps, with crisp text and plenty of room for split-screen views and floating windows.
 The audio doesn't go incredibly loud, but it stays clear and avoids growing harsh across nearly all its volume range, while there's a fairly wide stereo spread. Using the Googlebook in video meetings, we had no problems hearing others or being heard, and the 1080p camera captured clear, well-exposed video even when the lighting wasn't bright.
 Acer Googlebook 14: Software
 Acer's hardware is great, but it's Google's software that's really going to make or break the Googlebook. Googlebook OS, which now seems to be the official name, sees Google shifting focus away from the web and browser-based approach of Chrome OS to what's effectively a desktop-friendly spin on Android. Some aspects, like the way windows are handled or the toolbar, still feel very much like Chrome OS, but it uses the same Material 3 Expressive design language as Android 17 and gives Android apps the same prominence that Chrome OS gave Progressive Web Apps. Most importantly, it has a comprehensive file manager, to the extent that you can finally add folders to your desktop, creating the kind of barely organised mess that many MacOS and Windows owners know and love.
 Some Chromebook users were delighted to throw away the old desktop paradigms, but if you never quite gelled with the purely cloud-focused approach, Googlebook OS can feel more straightforward and usable. You can keep using PWAs and Google Drive where that fits into your workflows, and bring in Android apps and local files where that makes more sense to you. The interface isn't a huge departure from MacOS or Windows, and multitasking features work well. The Android 17 widgets, which you can use AI to create yourself, are great for keeping crucial info in your eyeline, even if the local AI powering them can't always access the services and data that you'd like it to.
 (Image credit: Future)
 However, two things make Googlebook OS distinct. Firstly, Gemini is even more embedded here than it was with Chrome OS on Chromebook Plus devices. The app sits on the toolbar, while content-creation and summary features are never further than a two-fingered tap or a prod of the Quick Insert key away. The AI-powered Rambler voice dictation feature doesn't just accurately recognise what you say, but strips out all your awkward 'ums' and 'errs' and spots when you self-correct. Wiggle the cursor over a section of text or an image on a Web page, and it comes up with context-sensitive prompts to explain or summarize the text or talk about symbolism in the picture. Googlebook OS surfaces AI tools in a useful and appropriate way that Windows Copilot+ has never really mastered.
 Secondly, it's designed to work in concert with Android smartphones. Pair the two and, provided both are working on the same Wi-Fi network, you can run your phone's apps on your Googlebook screen, read and respond to messages, and even pass tasks from your phone to your Googlebook. If there's something slightly magic about using smartphone apps you've not actually installed on your Googlebook, that goes double when you switch from your phone to your laptop and find you can carry on with your current browser page or app, just where you left off. It would be even better if it worked every time with every app, but it's still impressive.
 App support is still Google's biggest issue. Googlebook OS improves on Chrome OS by having 'built for desktop' and 'optimised for desktop' apps that support the desktop UI and don't feel so much like smartphone or tablet apps. Some, like the desktop versions of Luminar or LumaFusion, actually operate like useful and functional desktop apps that you can use to get real work done. However, there's no ignoring that the Android versions of Adobe and Microsoft's apps remain reduced-functionality mobile versions, or that you're better off using Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 in your productivity workflows than the more restrictive Android apps. This won't be a problem for Workspace users, but if you're in a primarily Microsoft Office-based or Adobe-based environment, Googlebooks aren't a natural fit any more than Chromebooks were.
 Acer Googlebook 14: Performance
 There's certainly nothing wrong with the performance of the Googlebook 14. We've tested the £1099 Core Ultra 7 355 configuration rather than the £999 Core Ultra 5 325 version, but it feels snappy and delivers benchmark results in line with what we'd expect from the Panther Lake chip. Due to the OS we can't run any Windows benchmarks, but it scores 2487 (single-core) and 11457 (multi-core) in Geekbench, which is in the same ballpark as the Windows-based Dell 16S, which uses the same chip. The score of 1773 in 3DMark's Steel Nomad (light) test is nothing to write home about, while the score of 20866 in Geekbench's GPU Compute test is equally mediocre. Still, the Googlebook 14 isn't likely to be employed as a graphics workstation or moonlight as a games machine.
 (Image credit: Future)
 Battery life is arguably more important, but in our usual video rundown test the Googlebook 14 lasted just only nine minutes over 14 hours. That's not a terrible result, and in a week of working the Googlebook 14 made it to the end of the working day without a recharge. All the same, it sometimes needed to be plugged in again if we had to carry on working in the evening. In this respect it's slightly behind the pace for lightweight Windows laptops, and it's going to be interesting to see how other Googlebooks compare.
 Acer Googlebook 14: Is it worth it?
 There are a lot of ways in which the Googlebook seems like a big step forward from the Chromebook. The Gemini and Android smartphone integration is just what we'd like to see in a forward-looking laptop. The desktop UI, apps, and file manager make it feel more like a versatile PC and less like a browser-based device with aspirations to do more.
 All the same, there's a sense that the wider app ecosystem isn't really where it needs to be yet, and some inconsistencies and occasional glitches spoil the experience. Acer's hardware is fantastic, and a great way to trial Googlebooks without investing too much. However, while Google's software shows a lot of potential, it works best if you're already invested in Android, cloud-native apps, and the wider Google ecosystem. For some enterprises, that's going to be a barrier.

 Best dual-HDMI office KVM: TESmart HKS202-P23 
 Best DisplayPort KVM for gaming: TESmart DKS202-M24 
 Best KVM for one laptop and one desktop: TESmart HDC202-X24

 Map the setup before choosing a KVM 
 The specifications that actually matter

 When a USB switch is the better buy 
 Common mistakes

 FAQ 
 Final recommendation 
 Sources and methodology 
 Buying a dual-monitor KVM switch backwards is expensive. The product name might promise two computers and two 4K displays, but that tells you almost nothing about whether it fits your desk.
 The useful questions are more specific: does each computer have two HDMI outputs, two DisplayPort outputs, or one Thunderbolt port? Do you need 4K at 60Hz or a high-refresh gaming display? Does the switch preserve display information when you change computers? Can your laptop drive two external displays in the first place?
 This guide is research-based. We have not completed hands-on testing of every KVM below. The recommendations are based on current manufacturer documentation, Amazon product-page checks, connection topology, stated display support, EDID features, included ports, and the setup each model is designed to solve.
 Quick picks: buy the TESmart HKS202-P23 for a straightforward two-computer, two-HDMI-monitor office setup. Buy the TESmart DKS202-M24 for two DisplayPort desktops and high-refresh displays. Buy the TESmart HDC202-X24 only when you specifically need to switch one Thunderbolt 4 laptop and one desktop through the same dual-monitor desk. The UGREEN dual-DisplayPort KVM is the cheaper DisplayPort option if you can live without hotkey switching or EDID emulation.
 Before choosing a laptop setup, use our dual-monitor KVM cable and compatibility checklist to map video feeds, dock outputs, USB data and charging.
 If a switch is already on the desk but a monitor stays dark, drops to 60Hz, or moves every window after a changeover, use our KVM black-screen troubleshooting order before replacing hardware.
 Our HKS202-P23 vs DKS202-M24 comparison maps the HDMI-versus-DisplayPort decision directly.
 Quick comparison
 Scroll horizontally to compare all 5 columns →
 Pick Host setup it suits Display connection Main reason to buy Main trade-off 
 TESmart HKS202-P23 Two desktops or laptops with two HDMI outputs each Dual HDMI Straightforward 4K60 office switching with EDID emulation Needs two HDMI feeds from each computer 
 TESmart DKS202-M24 Two DisplayPort desktops Dual DisplayPort 1.4 Higher refresh-rate headroom, EDID emulation, and included DP input cables Poor fit for a laptop unless its dock exposes two suitable DP outputs 
 TESmart HDC202-X24 One Thunderbolt 4 laptop and one desktop TB4 laptop input plus desktop HDMI/DP input Purpose-built hybrid topology with laptop charging and shared desk ports Expensive, and 60W charging is not enough for every laptop 
 UGREEN dual-monitor DisplayPort KVM Two DisplayPort computers Dual DisplayPort Lower-cost route to sharing two DP monitors and four USB devices No hotkey switching or EDID emulation; display support depends on the full signal chain 
 The table is a starting point, not a compatibility guarantee. Resolution and refresh-rate claims assume that the source computer, graphics output, KVM, cables, and monitors all support the required bandwidth and features.
 Who this guide is for
 Buy a dual-monitor KVM if:
 you regularly switch one keyboard, mouse, and two displays between two computers
 changing both monitor inputs manually is slowing you down
 you want USB peripherals to follow the active computer
 window rearrangement after switching is a recurring problem and you want EDID emulation
 you have mapped every host and monitor port before buying
 Skip a dual-monitor KVM if:
 you use one monitor and only need to share a keyboard and mouse
 your monitors already have enough inputs and a simple USB switch solves the peripheral problem
 one computer cannot natively drive two external displays
 you expect a KVM to add display support that the laptop or operating system does not have
 your gaming setup depends on a resolution, refresh rate, VRR mode, HDR format, or DSC path that the KVM documentation does not explicitly support
 If you are still choosing the displays, start with our best work monitors or best 32-inch 4K monitors guides. A monitor with a useful built-in KVM may remove the need for a separate box.
 Best dual-HDMI office KVM: TESmart HKS202-P23
 The TESmart HKS202-P23 is the cleanest recommendation when both computers can provide two HDMI outputs and both monitors accept HDMI. TESmart specifies dual-monitor switching for two computers, up to 4K at 60Hz, USB 3.0 peripheral sharing, audio connections, hotkey and button controls, and EDID emulators.
 That last feature matters on a work desk. EDID is the display information a computer uses to understand which monitors are connected and which modes they support. A KVM with EDID emulation can keep the displays visible to the inactive computer, reducing the chance that windows collapse onto one screen whenever you switch away. It does not guarantee perfect behavior with every computer, monitor, or operating system, but it is more useful than buying on the largest resolution number alone.
 The HKS202-P23 is not a one-cable laptop dock. Each host needs two HDMI video connections plus USB for peripheral switching. A laptop with one USB-C port will need a compatible dock or adapter that can expose the required outputs, and the laptop still needs native support for two external displays.
 Buy this if you have a conventional dual-HDMI office setup and want a clearly documented switching path. Skip it if either host is DisplayPort-first, you need a one-cable Thunderbolt laptop connection, or your main monitor runs above the modes TESmart documents.
 For the exact cable count, EDID limitations, per-screen mode, hotkey behavior, and laptop caveats, read our TESmart HKS202-P23 review .
 Best dual-HDMI office pick 
 TESmart HKS202-P23 Dual-Monitor HDMI KVM
 Why it works
 + Purpose-built for two computers and two HDMI monitors 
 + EDID emulation helps retain display information 
 + USB 3.0, button, remote, and hotkey switching 
 Main trade-off
 − Requires two HDMI outputs from each host 
 − 4K60 class rather than a high-refresh 4K gaming solution 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Best DisplayPort KVM for gaming: TESmart DKS202-M24
 The TESmart DKS202-M24 is the more appropriate pick for two DisplayPort desktops connected to high-refresh monitors. TESmart documents DisplayPort 1.4, EDID emulation, USB 3.x peripheral sharing, Gigabit Ethernet, audio, and advertised support up to 8K60 or 4K144-class modes depending on the signal chain.
 Treat those headline figures as ceilings, not promises. High-resolution, high-refresh output may depend on Display Stream Compression, cable quality, graphics-card output, monitor input support, color depth, HDR, and whether adaptive sync remains available in the chosen mode. Check the exact resolution and refresh-rate combination you use rather than assuming that an “8K” label covers everything below it.
 This is also a cable-heavy product. Two computers feeding two monitors means four DisplayPort input connections before the two monitor outputs and USB host connections are counted. TESmart lists the required host-side DisplayPort and USB cables with the kit, which reduces one source of ambiguity, but you should still plan the physical routing before buying.
 Buy this if both computers are DisplayPort desktops and keeping high-refresh display support is worth paying for. Skip it if your second machine is a USB-C laptop and you want one cable to handle video, peripherals, and charging.
 Our TESmart DKS202-M24 review maps the six DisplayPort runs, EDID behavior, published high-refresh ceilings, included cables, and laptop limitations before you buy.
 Best DisplayPort gaming pick 
 TESmart DKS202-M24 DisplayPort KVM
 Why it works
 + DisplayPort 1.4 topology for two dual-monitor desktops 
 + EDID emulation and higher refresh-rate headroom 
 + USB sharing, Ethernet, audio, and included host cables 
 Main trade-off
 − Expensive and cable-heavy 
 − Maximum display modes depend on the complete DP signal chain 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Best KVM for one laptop and one desktop: TESmart HDC202-X24
 The TESmart HDC202-X24 exists for the awkward setup most cheaper KVMs do not solve cleanly: one Thunderbolt 4 laptop, one desktop, and two shared monitors.
 TESmart specifies a Thunderbolt 4 connection for the laptop side, separate HDMI and DisplayPort connections for the desktop side, dual 4K60-class display support, EDID emulation, shared USB ports, Gigabit Ethernet, audio, and up to 60W charging for the connected laptop. This is much closer to a KVM and dock combined than a basic video switch.
 The topology is the reason to buy it, but it is also the reason to be careful. The laptop needs a compatible Thunderbolt connection and native support for the required number of external displays. Apple’s current guidance says external-display support varies by Mac model, resolution, and refresh rate. A KVM cannot increase that native limit. Windows laptops also vary, even when their USB-C ports look identical.
 The 60W charging figure deserves attention. It is enough for many thin-and-light laptops during normal work, but larger mobile workstations and performance laptops may charge slowly, reduce performance, or still require their original power adapter under load. Check the laptop manufacturer’s power requirement before treating this as a complete one-cable replacement.
 Buy this if you specifically have one compatible TB4 laptop and one HDMI/DisplayPort desktop. Skip it if both computers are ordinary desktops, both are USB-C laptops, or the price is close to replacing a monitor with one that has a built-in KVM.
 Our TESmart HDC202-X24 review maps the asymmetric host wiring, Mac display checks, 60W charging limit, shared ports, and split-screen mode before you buy.
 Best laptop + desktop pick 
 TESmart HDC202-X24 Thunderbolt 4 KVM
 Why it works
 + Designed for one TB4 laptop and one desktop 
 + Dual-display switching with EDID emulation 
 + Shared USB, Ethernet, audio, and 60W laptop charging 
 Main trade-off
 − Premium price 
 − 60W charging and dual-display support will not suit every laptop 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Best value dual-DisplayPort KVM: UGREEN
 UGREEN’s dual-monitor DisplayPort KVM is the simpler value option for two computers with two DisplayPort outputs each. UGREEN specifies support for two computers and two monitors, four shared USB 3.0 ports, DisplayPort 1.4, a front button, and a wired desktop controller. UGREEN explicitly lists no hotkey switching and no EDID emulation.
 Our dedicated UGREEN 55851 DisplayPort KVM review maps the six DP cables, missing EDID emulation, high-refresh caveats, and laptop requirements before you buy.
 The appeal is straightforward: it covers the common dual-DisplayPort topology without the price or larger feature set of the TESmart DKS202-M24. That makes sense for a productivity desk where you want both screens and common USB peripherals to follow the active desktop.
 The main work-desk trade-off is missing EDID emulation: the inactive computer may see disconnected monitors, so do not buy this to solve window rearrangement. UGREEN advertises high resolution and refresh-rate support, but buyers should still validate the exact mode, cables, graphics outputs, monitors, and adaptive-sync requirements. If persistent display identity and carefully documented EDID behavior are central to the purchase, the TESmart is the safer model to research first.
 Buy this if you want a lower-cost dual-DisplayPort switch and button or wired-controller switching is enough. Skip it if you need hotkeys, EDID emulation to help preserve your window layout, a one-cable laptop input, or the strongest available documentation for a high-refresh gaming chain.

 Computer B HDMI, DisplayPort, or USB-C/TB Second video output if required USB-A/B, USB-C, or TB Resolution + refresh rate 
 Monitor 1 HDMI or DisplayPort input Spare input if bypassing KVM n/a Resolution + refresh rate 
 Monitor 2 HDMI or DisplayPort input Spare input if bypassing KVM n/a Resolution + refresh rate 
 The host topology must match the KVM. A dual-HDMI KVM normally needs two HDMI feeds from each computer. A dual-DisplayPort KVM needs two DP feeds. USB-C does not automatically mean video, charging, Thunderbolt, or two-display support.
 If your laptop is the difficult part, our best laptop docking stations and Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 dock guide explain the port differences. Avoid stacking a dock and KVM unless both vendors document the intended setup; every added link makes compatibility harder to predict.
 The specifications that actually matter
 EDID emulation
 EDID tells a computer which display is connected and which modes it supports. Without persistent display information, switching away can look like physically unplugging the monitors. Windows may move, desktops can rearrange, and applications can reopen on the wrong screen.
 EDID emulation is worth paying for when display arrangement matters. It is not a guarantee against every wake, firmware, graphics-driver, or operating-system issue. If your picture returns but your apps move, our guide to KVM window rearrangement and persistent display detection explains what to check before paying for an emulator or replacement.
 Resolution and refresh rate
 Ignore the largest number on the box until you find your exact mode. “8K60” does not automatically guarantee dual 4K144 with HDR, full color depth, VRR, and every graphics card. Bandwidth may depend on DSC and the capabilities of every component in the path.
 For office use, dual 4K60 is the sensible target. For gaming, confirm the precise resolution, refresh rate, HDR mode, adaptive-sync support, and cable specification.
 USB speed and device behavior
 A keyboard and mouse require little bandwidth. Webcams, capture devices, audio interfaces, and external SSDs are less forgiving. Check how many USB ports are shared, their stated speed, and whether the KVM provides enough power for bus-powered devices.
 Wireless receivers can also behave differently from simple wired devices. A product saying “keyboard and mouse support” is not proof that every Bluetooth adapter, multi-device receiver, macro keyboard, or gaming peripheral will switch perfectly.
 Charging power
 Charging only matters on KVMs with laptop docking features. Compare the KVM’s stated output with the laptop’s normal adapter. A 60W source can keep an efficient laptop running while still being a poor match for a mobile workstation that expects 100W or more.
 Cables in the box
 A dual-monitor KVM can require four host video cables, two display cables, two USB host cables, and power. Check what is included. Do not mix unverified adapters into a high-refresh path and then assume the KVM is the cause of every blank screen.
 MacBook compatibility: check the exact model
 Do not buy a dual-monitor KVM on the assumption that every MacBook can drive two external displays through one cable. Apple documents display limits by model, chip, resolution, and refresh rate. Some recent Macs support two external displays, while older or lower-tier models may have different limits or operating conditions.
 The KVM does not create an extra display engine. Confirm the Mac’s native external-display support first, then confirm that the KVM uses a connection method the Mac supports. Be especially careful with USB-C docks that rely on DisplayPort MST: a manufacturer may document different extended-display behavior for Windows and macOS.
 When a USB switch is the better buy
 You may not need a video KVM at all.
 If both monitors have two inputs, connect each computer directly to each monitor. Then use a basic USB switch for the keyboard, mouse, webcam, and other peripherals. Switching takes an extra button press or two, but the displays keep a direct signal path and you avoid paying for high-bandwidth video switching.
 Our USB switch vs KVM switch guide maps the wiring, high-refresh trade-offs, and the exact cases where saving money creates more daily friction.
 This approach is often better when:
 the primary display runs at a high refresh rate
 each monitor already has enough inputs
 you change computers only once or twice per day
 you want to keep VRR, HDR, or unusual display modes out of the KVM path
 the KVM that matches the exact topology costs more than the inconvenience is worth
 An ultrawide with a built-in KVM is another clean alternative. Our best ultrawide monitors guide includes work-focused models with USB-C, Ethernet, and KVM features.
 For the rest of the desk, our ergonomic workstation guide covers monitor placement, input devices, lighting, and cable planning.
 Common mistakes
 Counting KVM outputs but not host inputs: two monitor outputs do not mean one cable from each computer. Many dual-monitor KVMs need two video feeds per host.
 Assuming every USB-C port carries video: USB-C describes the connector. The port may lack DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt, charging input, or the required multi-display support.
 Buying on “8K” branding: your exact dual-monitor mode matters more than the maximum single-display headline.
 Ignoring EDID: a cheaper switch may move every window when you change computers. That becomes annoying quickly on a work desk.
 Expecting the KVM to fix a laptop display limit: the computer must support the number and type of displays before the switch enters the picture.
 Using random cables and adapters: high-bandwidth display problems are often signal-chain problems. Use appropriately rated cables and keep the path simple.
 Alternatives to consider
 Monitor with a built-in KVM: best when you are replacing the display anyway and want fewer boxes.
 USB switch plus direct video inputs: cheaper and often safer for high-refresh monitors.
 Thunderbolt dock plus monitor input switching: useful when the laptop needs one-cable docking but video switching is occasional.
 Software keyboard and mouse sharing: suitable when you only need input sharing and both computers stay on the same network. It does not switch the monitors.
 Remote desktop: useful for administering a secondary computer, but not a replacement for direct display access in latency-sensitive or graphics-heavy work.
 FAQ
 Can a KVM switch run two extended monitors?
 Yes, if the KVM is designed for two monitors and each computer provides the required video signals. A dual-monitor KVM cannot make a computer support an extra display that it cannot drive natively.
 Do I need two video cables from each computer?
 Usually, for conventional HDMI or DisplayPort dual-monitor KVMs. Dock-style Thunderbolt or USB-C models may carry multiple display signals through one host cable, but only with compatible computers and documented display support.
 Is DisplayPort or HDMI better for a KVM?
 Use the interface that matches both computers and monitors. DisplayPort is the more natural fit for many high-refresh PC setups. HDMI is common on office monitors and laptops. Converting between them adds another compatibility point.
 Does a KVM add input lag?
 A correctly functioning digital KVM should not be treated like a game-streaming device, but we have not independently measured latency on these models. Competitive players should prioritize a documented high-refresh signal path and consider direct video connections with a separate USB switch if uncertainty is unacceptable.
 Why do my windows move after switching computers?
 The inactive computer may think its monitors were disconnected. EDID emulation can help keep display identity available during switching, although graphics drivers, operating-system behavior, monitor firmware, and sleep settings can still affect window placement.
 Our KVM black-screen and display-detection guide separates EDID symptoms from bandwidth, cable, dock, wake, and host-topology faults.
 Will a dual-monitor KVM work with a MacBook?
 Only if the exact MacBook supports the required external-display configuration and the KVM’s host connection matches it. Check Apple’s model-specific display documentation and the KVM manufacturer’s macOS notes before buying.
 Can I connect a dock to a KVM?
 Sometimes, but it adds another device to the video and USB chain. Use a dock-plus-KVM arrangement only when the required outputs, resolution, refresh rate, charging, and operating-system behavior are documented or returnable if incompatible.
 Final recommendation
 Buy the TESmart HKS202-P23 for a normal dual-HDMI office desk. It is the least complicated route when both hosts already provide the required HDMI outputs.
 Buy the TESmart DKS202-M24 for two DisplayPort desktops and high-refresh monitors. Pay for it because the topology and EDID features match the job, not because the box says 8K.
 Buy the TESmart HDC202-X24 only for its intended one-Thunderbolt-laptop, one-desktop setup. Check display support and charging requirements first.
 Buy the UGREEN dual-DisplayPort KVM when you want the basic dual-DP job done for less and do not need hotkeys or EDID emulation.

 What to Look for in a KVM Switch for a Laptop and Desktop
 Key buying criteria so you get the right fit the first time.
 01 Verify EDID emulation is included, regardless of price
 EDID (Extended Display Identification Data) is the information a monitor sends to a connected computer describing its supported resolutions and refresh rates, and a KVM switch without EDID emulation can cause a real, recurring annoyance: when you switch away from a computer, that computer loses its connection to the monitor's EDID data, and some graphics drivers respond by dropping to a default low resolution or losing the display arrangement entirely until you manually reconfigure it after switching back.
 A switch with proper EDID emulation stores and continuously presents the monitor's display information to every connected computer regardless of which one is actively selected, so switching back and forth doesn't repeatedly trigger resolution resets or display rearrangement.
 This feature isn't reliably tied to price, a budget switch can include it while a similarly priced competitor omits it, so check the listing or current buyer reviews specifically for EDID emulation rather than assuming it based on price alone.
 02 Match USB peripheral support to what you actually plug in, not just keyboard and mouse
 0 or higher) vary significantly beyond that baseline, and this matters concretely if you also want to switch a USB webcam, external drive, audio interface, or other peripheral along with the computer selection rather than leaving it permanently connected to one machine.
 0 ports can handle a webcam or external drive at full speed as part of the same switching action.
 Count your actual USB peripherals beyond keyboard and mouse, and check both the port count and the stated USB generation against what those specific peripherals need to function at full speed.
 03 Check whether switching happens via hotkey, a physical button, or both, and whether that matches your workflow
 KVM switches offer switching through a physical button on the device itself, a keyboard hotkey combination (commonly a specific key pressed a set number of times), or both, and this is a genuine day-to-day usability factor rather than a minor detail, since a physical button requires reaching across or behind your desk setup every time you switch, while hotkey switching lets you change computers without moving your hands from the keyboard at all.
 This matters more the more frequently you actually switch between computers during a session, someone switching once or twice a day may not care, while someone switching dozens of times while referencing one machine and working on another benefits meaningfully from hotkey support.
 Check whether hotkey switching is explicitly supported and confirm the specific key combination works with your operating system, since some hotkey implementations have compatibility quirks on certain OS versions.
 04 Confirm audio switching is included if you need it, since many KVM switches handle video and USB but not audio
 A significant number of KVM switches route video and USB peripherals between computers but do not switch audio output at all, meaning your speakers or headphones stay connected to whichever computer they were originally plugged into regardless of which computer is currently selected for video and keyboard control, a confusing experience if you're not expecting it.
 This is a distinct, separately-implemented feature, not something that comes automatically bundled with video and USB switching, so a switch's audio support (or lack of it) needs to be checked explicitly rather than assumed.
 If you regularly use audio output and want it to follow the same switching action as your monitor and keyboard, check the listing specifically for stated audio switching support rather than assuming any KVM switch handles this by default.
 05 Check physical port placement and cable routing, since a technically capable switch can still be annoying to use daily
 Beyond core specs like resolution support and port count, the physical layout of a KVM switch's ports on its housing meaningfully affects how pleasant it is to actually live with on a desk: ports crammed close together can make thick HDMI or USB-C cables difficult to seat fully, and ports facing an awkward direction relative to how the switch sits on or under your desk can turn routine cable management into a recurring frustration that a spec sheet never reveals.
 This is exactly the kind of detail that only shows up in real photos of the actual unit or in buyer reviews mentioning cable fit and port spacing, not in the resolution and port-count specs that dominate most listings.
 Look at actual product photos showing port placement and spacing before buying, and check reviews specifically for mentions of cable clearance issues if you're using thicker high-speed cables.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do my laptop and desktop connect to a KVM switch the same way?

 You'll likely dock and undock the laptop daily while the desktop stays permanently connected, EDID emulation keeps your resolution and layout consistent across those reconnects.

 It's a helpful compatibility signal, stronger than a switch marketed generically for two identical computer sources.

 It can if power delivery is included, verify the specific wattage matches your laptop's charging requirement.

results.text:
Best KVM Switches for Dual Monitor Setups (2026) | Dock Gear HQ 
 Disclosure: Some links in this article are affiliate links. We may earn a commission on qualifying purchases at no extra cost to you.
 Most dual-monitor KVM listings lead with a single number — 8K60, 4K144, 4K240 — and let you assume it applies to both screens at once. For a dual-monitor setup, that assumption is the most expensive one you can make: a KVM rated 4K120 on one output can behave very differently once two displays are live simultaneously. This guide is built around that gap.
 Three distinct setups hide behind the same search. In the first, two desktop PCs each feed two video cables into the switch. In the second, a laptop and a desktop share two monitors, and the laptop should ideally arrive over a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable. In the third, two laptops share the desk and an integrated KVM dock is the cleaner answer. A fourth group is really searching for "one monitor, two computers" — and should know up front that a single-monitor KVM does not become a native dual-monitor KVM by adding another cable.
 For every pick below, four things are reported that most roundups skip: the documented simultaneous two-monitor ceiling rather than the per-output maximum, EDID behavior, how many cables each computer actually needs, and how the unit behaves on a Mac. Those four factors decide whether a desk switches cleanly or fights you at every changeover.
 This is written for anyone running two monitors across two machines — a MacBook, a Dell XPS, a desktop tower, or a mix — who wants one keyboard and mouse without giving up resolution, refresh rate, or window layout.

 What Makes a Great Dual-Monitor KVM?
 Five specifications separate a switch that works from one that quietly degrades your desk.
 The simultaneous dual-display ceiling, not a single-output headline. A box advertising 8K60 or 4K240 may only sustain that on one active link. The only figure that matters for a dual-monitor buyer is what both outputs can hold at once. Cable Matters' 201075 is the clearest example: its genuine two-monitor ceiling is 2× 3840×2160@60, while the 8K30 figure belongs to a single-display mode. Those are not the same promise.
 EDID emulation. EDID tells a computer what a monitor can do. A KVM with persistent EDID keeps telling the inactive computer "the monitor is still here," which reduces resolution resets, desktop icon shuffling and window rearrangement on every switch. Several strong products skip it: UGREEN's 55851 and Cable Matters' 201075 both document no EDID emulation, and Level1Techs states plainly that its KVM does not emulate the monitor as permanently connected. USB/HID emulation — as implemented on StarTech's unit — is a different feature and should not be read as display EDID support.
 Cables per host. A conventional dual-monitor KVM typically needs two video cables plus one USB cable from every computer. A USB-C KVM dock needs one. A hybrid laptop-plus-desktop model needs one cable from the laptop and three from the desktop. That count decides how much of your desk disappears behind the monitors.
 The Mac topology question. macOS does not use ordinary USB-C DisplayPort MST to create two independent extended desktops the way Windows does. Docks that rely on MST — AV Access, Anker and Cable Matters among them — therefore document mirrored external screens on macOS even while producing dual extended 4K on Windows. A KVM cannot manufacture display engines the Mac does not expose. Support also depends on the exact chip and model: the original M1 MacBook Air natively drives one external display up to 6K60, while current M4-generation MacBook Pro configurations can natively drive two, and higher-end Max configurations more depending on mode.
 Where the bandwidth actually gets spent. At 4K120 and above, with HDR or DSC, the whole link budget matters: cable length and certification, passive or active adapters, dock-to-KVM chains, DSC and HDCP negotiation, DP link training, and the source port's own headroom. A common field report is that a direct GPU DisplayPort connection works while the identical path through a dock or adapter fails — even as USB peripherals keep switching normally.

 The Modular Route: A USB Switch Plus a DisplayLink Dock
 Not every desk needs a new KVM. If you already own a good USB docking station, the Plugable pattern — a USB 3.0 switch in front of a DisplayLink dock — is deliberately a two-product architecture rather than a single KVM, and it solves the "I already own a dock" question cheaply.
 Plugable USB3-SWITCH2 — a 2-host USB 3 / 5Gbps switch with a hardware pushbutton and no hotkey requirement, switching the entire attached USB device tree.
 Plugable UD-6950Z — a DisplayLink USB graphics dock with two display groups over HDMI 2.0 / DisplayPort 1.2, running two 4K60 displays simultaneously, with six USB-A 5Gbps ports, Gigabit Ethernet and 3.5mm audio.
 The topology is computer → USB switch → DisplayLink dock → monitors and peripherals. There is no Power Delivery, so laptops keep their own chargers.
 Why it stands out: It can work around some Mac native-display limits because the extra displays are software-driven rather than native streams, and it is materially cheaper than replacing an entire dock.
 Watch out for: DisplayLink is not equivalent to native DisplayPort Alt Mode. It requires the DisplayLink driver on the host, processes video in software, is unsuitable for some protected-content paths, and is not the architecture for latency-sensitive or high-refresh gaming. The USB3-SWITCH2 is also not intended to switch arbitrary USB-C or Thunderbolt Alt Mode docks — it is a USB graphics solution.

 One Monitor, Two Computers: What Actually Works
 The "KVM switch, one monitor, two computers" search deserves a straight answer: a single-monitor KVM does not become a native dual-monitor KVM just because you add a second display. A single-monitor DisplayPort 1.4 switch with 8K60 and 4K240-class single-display modes and four USB 3.0 ports will control one monitor and your USB peripherals — and that is all it will do.
 If you need a second screen in that setup, there are two honest options:
 Connect the second monitor directly to each PC using separate inputs on the monitor, and let the KVM control only monitor #1 and USB.
 Manage the second display through a second video switch or dock. 
 Both are economically rational, but switching is less unified and window and EDID behavior gets more complex — two changeover actions instead of one. A third option skips video switching entirely: connect both computers directly to both monitors, use each monitor's built-in input selector, and buy only a USB peripheral switch . That removes a high-bandwidth KVM from the video chain altogether at the cost of a few extra button presses when changing machines.

 Which Dual-Monitor KVM Should You Buy?
 Match the wiring reality of your desk to the pick, not the other way around.
 Two desktop PCs, high-refresh DisplayPort monitors. TESmart DKS202-M24-USBK. If the displays are HDMI instead, the HKS202-M24-V2-USBK is its direct equivalent.
 Two desktops, 4K60 office work. ATEN CS1842 for HDMI desks that need display-state management, IOGEAR GCS1942 where firmware lifecycle matters most, or StarTech's P2DD46A2 for a corporate fleet.
 Budget dual-DisplayPort workstation. UGREEN 55851 — accepting the lack of EDID and hotkeys in exchange for the price.
 Three or four computers. IOGEAR/ATEN CS1944DPA, since serious dual-display KVM lines rarely offer a dedicated three-host chassis.
 Thunderbolt laptops. Sabrent SB-TB4K, provided your hosts are genuinely Thunderbolt-certified.
 Work laptop plus gaming desktop. TESmart HDC202-X24-USBK at the top end, AV Access KD-E10 for the better-value version.
 Two laptops sharing the desk. AV Access iDock C20, Cable Matters 201075, or the Anker 554 for Windows machines.
 You already own a good dock. Adding a conventional KVM is more modular and easier to replace independently than swapping the whole dock. If your dock is a DisplayLink model , the Plugable USB switch pattern is materially cheaper than replacement.
 Mac plus PC. Validate the Mac's exact native external-display count first. USB-C MST alone will not solve macOS dual-extension limits, and a KVM cannot add display engines the Mac does not expose.
 Gaming at 1440p240 or 4K120 and above. Prefer direct DisplayPort or HDMI into a native-video KVM. DisplayLink's software video path brings driver dependency and compression that works against latency-sensitive play.
 The three wiring experiences are worth stating plainly, because "KVM with docking station" means very different things depending on which one you are buying. A conventional dual-monitor KVM takes two video cables plus one USB cable from every computer. A dual-laptop KVM dock takes a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable per laptop. A hybrid laptop-plus-desktop KVM dock takes one cable from the laptop and dedicated video plus USB from the desktop.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Q: Can a single-monitor KVM switch two monitors? 
 No. A single-monitor KVM controls one display and your USB peripherals, and it does not become a native dual-monitor KVM by adding a second cable. To drive a second screen you either connect it directly to each computer using separate monitor inputs, route it through a second switch, or skip video switching entirely and use each monitor's built-in input selector.
 Q: Does a dual-monitor KVM work with a Mac? 
 It depends on the model and the Mac. macOS does not use ordinary USB-C DisplayPort MST to create two independent extended desktops, so MST-based dock/KVMs — including the AV Access iDock C20, the Anker 554 and the Cable Matters 201075 — document mirrored external screens on Macs even though they produce dual extended 4K on Windows. Native-display products such as the Sabrent SB-TB4K behave differently, but only where the specific Mac actually exposes the required number of display streams. Original M1 MacBook Air machines natively drive one external display; current M4-generation MacBook Pro configurations can drive two, and Max configurations more depending on mode.
 Q: What is the difference between a KVM switch and a KVM dock? 
 A conventional KVM switch routes video from two cables per computer plus a USB link, and it does not charge the host. A KVM dock combines the switch with docking-station connectivity — USB hubs, Ethernet, card readers and Power Delivery — and often reduces each laptop to a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable. Hybrid models serve one laptop plus one desktop, giving the laptop a single cable while the desktop still supplies dedicated video and USB connections.
 Q: Why does my dual-monitor KVM drop to a lower resolution than advertised? 
 Almost always because the advertised figure is a single-output maximum, not a simultaneous two-display ceiling. A KVM listed at 8K60 or 4K240 may only sustain that on one active link. At 4K120 and above the full link budget also matters: cable length and certification, adapters, dock-to-KVM chains, DSC and HDCP negotiation, DP link training, and the source port's own headroom can each reduce what both monitors receive at once.
 Q: Do I need EDID emulation in a dual-monitor KVM? 
 It depends on how much you dislike redoing your desktop. Persistent EDID emulation keeps telling the inactive computer that the monitors are still attached, which reduces resolution resets, icon movement and window rearrangement on each switch. Without it, the operating system is far more likely to treat the monitors as physically unplugged. Note that USB or HID emulation is a separate feature and does not provide display EDID persistence.
 Q: How many cables does a dual-monitor KVM need per computer? 
 A conventional dual-monitor KVM typically needs two video cables plus one USB cable from every computer. A dual-laptop KVM dock needs a single USB-C or Thunderbolt cable per laptop, though the monitors may still require adapters depending on their inputs. A hybrid laptop-plus-desktop model needs one cable from the laptop and three from the desktop — DisplayPort or HDMI plus USB.
 Q: Will a dual-monitor KVM work through my existing USB-C dock? 
 Sometimes, but the dock-to-KVM chain is a known failure point. Users regularly report that a direct GPU DisplayPort or HDMI connection works while the identical display path through a dock or adapter fails, even though USB peripherals keep switching normally. If you already own a high-quality dock, feeding a conventional KVM from the dock's outputs is workable, but test the full chain before committing to a high-refresh configuration.
 Q: Is DisplayLink good enough for a dual-monitor KVM setup? 
 For office work and multiple screens, yes. DisplayLink creates displays through software and a host driver rather than a native GPU stream, which makes it useful when a computer cannot expose the number of native displays you want — including some Mac limitations. It brings trade-offs: driver dependency, software processing and compression, weaker suitability for latency-sensitive gaming, and protected-content limitations on some workflows. For gaming, native DisplayPort or Thunderbolt video is the better path.
 Conclusion
 The right dual-monitor KVM comes down to four numbers, not one. Check the simultaneous two-monitor ceiling rather than the single-output headline, confirm whether EDID emulation is present, count the cables each computer will need, and know how your operating system handles multiple external displays — especially on macOS, where USB-C MST does not produce two independent extended desktops.
 If you want one recommendation that covers the most demanding conventional desk, the TESmart DKS202-M24-USBK is the pick: dual DisplayPort 1.4, smart EDID, and a documented dual 8K60 / dual 4K144 ceiling stated separately from its per-output modes. For an HDMI desk, the HKS202-M24-V2 is its direct equivalent. For office and professional deployments, the ATEN CS1842 and IOGEAR GCS1942 trade headline refresh for display-state management and a real support lifecycle. If Thunderbolt laptops are the target, the Sabrent SB-TB4K is the cleanest one-cable answer, and on a tighter budget the UGREEN 55851 remains the cheapest credible route to two DisplayPort monitors.
 The most common mistake is not buying the wrong brand but buying the wrong category: a laptop-plus-desktop user needs a hybrid dock/KVM , a two-laptop user needs an integrated KVM dock, and a two-desktop user needs a conventional two-video-cable switch. Match the category first, then the specification.

results.title: 165 Hz Becomes 120: Best KVM Switch for Laptop and Desktop
results.text:
165 Hz Becomes 120: Best KVM Switch for Laptop and Desktop 
 Skip to content 
 This article contains affiliate links. We may earn a commission if you buy through our links, at no extra cost to you. 
 The best KVM switch for laptop and desktop sharing on one monitor is the UGREEN aluminum HDMI KVM at about $48: one button moves your screen, keyboard, mouse and four USB 3.0 devices between two computers. What it will not do is the part most buyers assume it does.
 A KVM switch shares a desk; it does not replace a dock. It will not charge your laptop, and its video chip sets a ceiling on refresh rate that a gaming monitor can easily exceed.
 We compared published specs, current amazon.com prices and owner feedback on the KVM switches that sell for mixed work and gaming desks, and these three each fit a different setup.
 Refresh rate settles this one. The basic UGREEN lists 4K at 60 Hz and 1440p at up to 120 Hz, so a 144 or 165 Hz monitor drops to 120 through it, and the aluminum UGREEN is rated at 4K 60 Hz. The TESmart supports 4K at 60 Hz and 3,440 by 1,440 at 100 Hz.
 Quick Answer 
 The UGREEN Aluminum HDMI KVM Switch is the best KVM for one monitor and two computers: 4K at 60 Hz and four USB 3.0 ports for about $48. For two monitors, EDID emulation and hotkeys, get the TESmart Dual Monitor DP + HDMI KVM at about $229. On a budget, the UGREEN HDMI KVM Switch does the basics with USB 2.0 ports for about $30.
 Table of Contents
 Toggle 
 A KVM Switch Shares a Desk, It Does Not Dock a Laptop 
 A KVM switch takes one monitor, keyboard and mouse and moves them between two computers at the press of a button. That is the whole job, and for a work laptop and a personal desktop on one desk, it is exactly what you need.
 What it does not do is power the laptop. None of the switches here pass charging power to a computer, so the laptop still needs its own charger, and a USB-C laptop needs an HDMI or DisplayPort adapter or cable to connect.
 If you only use one computer at a time and want a single cable to the laptop, a dock is the better tool. Our USB-C docking stations cover that route.
 A Gaming Monitor Can Lose Refresh Rate Through a KVM 
 The video chip inside a KVM switch has its own limits, and your signal passes through it. The basic UGREEN lists 4K at 60 Hz and 2,560 by 1,440 at up to 120 Hz, so a 1440p monitor that runs at 144 or 165 Hz on its own drops to 120 through the switch.
 For office work and most games, 120 Hz is still smooth. For competitive games where you paid for 165 Hz, it is a real loss, and the workaround is to plug the gaming PC straight into the monitor and use the KVM only for the keyboard and mouse.
 The TESmart is rated for 4K at 60 Hz and 3,440 by 1,440 at 100 Hz, so it suits ultrawide work monitors rather than fast gaming panels. Our ultrawide monitors for productivity cover screens in that range.
 EDID Emulation Stops Your Windows From Jumping 
 When a KVM switches away from a computer, that computer may think the monitor was unplugged. It then moves your open windows to its own screen, and when you switch back, they are scattered.
 EDID emulation fixes that by telling each computer the monitor is always there. The TESmart has EDID emulators on every input; both UGREEN switches state that they do not support EDID emulation.
 If you leave a dozen windows arranged on one machine, that difference matters every time you switch. If you mostly use full-screen apps, you may not notice. Our guide to setting up dual monitors covers display arrangements.
 Hotkeys and Remotes Decide How Often You Reach for the Switch 
 The two UGREEN switches change computers with a button on the box, and the basic model adds a wired desktop controller. The TESmart adds keyboard hotkeys and an IR remote, so you can switch without reaching for anything.
 Both UGREEN switches also state that they need both USB cables connected for power and data, so plan the cable runs to each computer. The aluminum UGREEN adds a USB-C power port for when you plug in high-power devices like external drives.
 If the switch sits behind the monitor, the desktop controller or the TESmart’s remote saves the most frustration.
 A laptop stand next to the monitor keeps the laptop’s own screen usable as a third display when it is the active computer.
 Three KVM Switches, and Who Should Skip Each One 
 UGREEN Aluminum HDMI KVM Switch — Best Overall 
 The aluminum UGREEN is the KVM to buy for a work laptop and a personal desktop on one monitor, at about $48 from UGREEN’s store. It shares one HDMI monitor at up to 4K 60 Hz between two computers, along with four USB 3.0 devices, such as a keyboard, a mouse, a webcam and an external drive.
 If you move files to an external drive from either computer, the USB 3.0 ports are the reason to pay about $18 more than the basic model, which runs its ports at USB 2.0 speed. The aluminum case looks at home on a desk, and a USB-C power input keeps high-power devices like drives running reliably.
 Where it falls short is features. It has no EDID emulation and no hotkey switching, so windows can move when you switch and you change computers with the button on the box. UGREEN also notes that both USB cables must be connected for it to work, so each computer needs a free USB port. It supports HDMI only, not DisplayPort, and it does not charge your laptop.
 Skip it if you run two monitors; the TESmart handles a dual-screen desk.
 TESmart Dual Monitor DP + HDMI KVM — Best for Two Monitors 
 The TESmart is the KVM for a two-monitor desk shared between two computers, at about $229 from TESmart’s store. It has one DisplayPort and one HDMI output, supports 4K at 60 Hz and 3,440 by 1,440 at 100 Hz, and includes EDID emulators on each input so your windows stay put.
 If you switch often, its three methods are the standout: a front button, keyboard hotkeys and an IR remote. Two USB 3.0 ports run at up to 5 Gbps, one of them can charge a phone, and Tesmart supports wired, wireless and gaming keyboards and mice. HDR10 and HDCP are supported, and the case is metal.
 The trade-offs are price and refresh rate. It costs nearly five times the UGREEN, and its rated modes top out at 100 Hz at 3,440 by 1,440, which does not suit a fast gaming monitor. It has only two USB 3.0 ports, so a busy desk may need a hub, and the IR remote needs AAA batteries that are not included.
 Skip it if you run one monitor; the UGREEN switches cost a fraction and do the same job for one screen.
 UGREEN HDMI KVM Switch — Best Budget 
 The basic UGREEN KVM is the cheapest way to share one monitor between two computers, at about $30 from UGREEN’s store. It supports HDMI 2.0 at 4K 60 Hz or 1440p at up to 120 Hz, HDR and HDCP 2.2, and four USB ports for a keyboard, a mouse and two more devices.
 If you only need to move a keyboard, mouse and screen between a work laptop and a home PC, it covers that, and the box includes two HDMI cables and two USB cables, so you can set it up without buying anything else. A desktop controller lets you switch from the desk even when the box is hidden.
 Where it falls short is speed and convenience. Its USB ports run at USB 2.0 speed, which is fine for a keyboard and mouse but slow for a drive, and like the aluminum model it has no EDID emulation and no hotkeys. Its plastic case feels lighter than the aluminum one.
 Skip it if you move large files between computers; the aluminum UGREEN’s USB 3.0 ports are about 10 times faster.
 Before You Buy 
 Does a KVM switch work with a laptop? 
 Yes, over HDMI or DisplayPort. A USB-C laptop needs a USB-C to HDMI or DisplayPort cable or adapter, plus a USB cable for the keyboard and mouse.
 Does a KVM switch charge your laptop? 
 None of these do. Keep the laptop’s charger plugged in, or use a dock instead if you only need one computer at a time. Our docking stations for dual monitors cover that option.
 Does a KVM switch add input lag? 
 Not noticeably for keyboards and mice in office work. The bigger effect is a lower refresh-rate ceiling on fast gaming monitors.
 The Call 
 The UGREEN aluminum HDMI KVM is the switch we would buy for one monitor and two computers, because it shares a 4K screen and four USB 3.0 ports for about $48. If your desk has two monitors, the TESmart’s EDID emulation and hotkeys are worth the extra money.

Best KVM Switch for 2 Computers (2026) | DeskDNA 
 Gear Guide
 Best KVM Switch for
2 Computers (2026)
 By DeskDNA Editorial Team · Reviewed September 2026 · How we test 
 If you run a work laptop and a personal or gaming PC at the same desk, a KVM switch lets both share one monitor, keyboard, and mouse — one button instead of a cable swap. The right pick depends on one question: does your monitor already have a spare input, and do you need 4K, high refresh, or laptop charging?
 Quick answer: The UGREEN HDMI KVM (~$70, 4K@60Hz, cables and controller included) is the best pick for most hybrid desks sharing one monitor. If your monitor already has two inputs, save money with a peripheral-only USB switch (~$40). Step up to a DisplayPort KVM (~$160) for 4K/144Hz, or a USB-C dock (~$200) if both machines are laptops.
 Affiliate disclosure: DeskDNA earns a small Amazon commission on qualifying purchases through “Shop” links on this page, at no extra cost to you. Commissions do not influence which products we recommend — see our editorial methodology .
 Best Budget UGREEN USB 3.0 Sharing Switch — Peripherals Only

 Why we chose it
 “ The cheapest correct answer for a lot of setups — if your monitor has two inputs, skip the video KVM and just share peripherals. ”
 Pros
 ✓ Shares one keyboard, mouse, and USB devices between two computers over USB 3.0 at 5Gbps — no video switching
 ✓ The right pick if your monitor already has two inputs: you toggle the display, this toggles everything else
 ✓ One button (or hotkey) moves all peripherals between both machines in about a second
 ✓ Plug-and-play with no drivers on Windows, macOS, and Linux, for around $40
 Trade-offs
 ✗ Does not switch the monitor — only useful if your display already has a spare HDMI or DisplayPort input
 ✗ No video path at all, so nothing to configure for 4K or high refresh; it is strictly a peripheral sharer
 Best for: Anyone whose monitor already has two video inputs and only needs to share a keyboard, mouse, and dock between two PCs.
 Best Overall UGREEN HDMI KVM — 2 PCs, 1 Monitor, 4K@60Hz
