 Check price › 
 Why we chose it
 “ Buy this first. One monitor, one keyboard, one mouse across two computers for around $70 — cables and controller included. ”
 Pros
 ✓ Switches one HDMI monitor plus keyboard, mouse, and four USB 3.0 devices between two computers with one button
 ✓ 4K@60Hz, plus 1440p@120Hz and 1080p@240Hz — covers office resolution and mainstream high-refresh gaming
 ✓ Ships with the desktop controller, two HDMI cables, and two USB cables — no separate $30 cable run to buy
 ✓ Aluminum body with HDR passthrough, plug-and-play with no drivers on any OS
 Trade-offs
 ✗ HDMI caps below the DisplayPort tier — no 4K@144Hz for high-refresh 4K gaming
 ✗ Single-monitor only; a dual-monitor KVM is a different, pricier box
 Best for: Most hybrid workers sharing one monitor between a work laptop and a personal or gaming PC.
 Best for High Refresh TESmart DisplayPort 1.4 KVM — 4K@144Hz, VRR
 $ 160
 Check price › 
 Why we chose it
 “ The pick when you own a 4K/144Hz DisplayPort monitor — the HDMI KVMs cannot carry that signal, this one can. ”
 Pros
 ✓ DisplayPort 1.4 carries 4K@144Hz (or 8K@60Hz) with VRR — G-Sync and FreeSync pass through for tear-free gaming
 ✓ EDID emulation stops your windows rearranging every time you switch machines — the flaw cheap boxes have
 ✓ SmartClip copies and pastes files directly between the two computers, no USB drive or cloud
 ✓ USB 3.0 peripheral ports plus dedicated audio and microphone jacks
 Trade-offs
 ✗ At ~$160 it is over double the HDMI pick — only worth it for 4K high-refresh or pro creative work
 ✗ DisplayPort-only inputs; a mixed HDMI-plus-DP setup needs the pricier HDMI+DP model
 Best for: Gamers and creators on a high-refresh 4K DisplayPort monitor who refuse to drop frames when switching machines.
 Best for Laptop Docking Cable Matters USB-C KVM Dock — 100W PD
 $ 200
 Check price › 
 Why we chose it
 “ The one to buy if both machines are laptops — a single USB-C cable each replaces a charger, a dongle, and a KVM at once. ”
 Pros
 ✓ One USB-C cable to each laptop carries video, USB peripherals, and up to 100W charging — dock and undock in a single plug
 ✓ Dual 4K@60Hz output over DisplayPort and HDMI — drives one or two monitors from either machine
 ✓ 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C ports for fast external drives, not just a keyboard and mouse
 ✓ Thunderbolt 4 compatible, so it works across a MacBook and a Windows laptop
 Trade-offs
 ✗ Built for two laptops, not desktops — a tower without USB-C video output cannot use the one-cable trick
 ✗ At ~$200 it is the most expensive here; overkill unless you genuinely dock and undock daily
 Best for: Two-laptop or laptop-plus-MacBook setups that want single-cable docking with charging, not just peripheral switching.
 What to check before you buy
 Do you need video? If your monitor has two inputs, a $40 peripheral switch is enough. If not, get an HDMI or DP video KVM. 
 Video standard HDMI covers 4K@60Hz / 1080p@240Hz. DisplayPort 1.4 is required for 4K@144Hz and VRR. 
 USB version USB 3.0 (5Gbps) for external drives and webcams. USB 2.0 boxes bottleneck fast peripherals. 
 Power delivery Only USB-C KVM docks charge a laptop (up to 100W). HDMI/DP KVMs carry no power. 
 EDID emulation Keeps windows from rearranging on every switch. Standard on better DP KVMs, rare on cheap ones. 
 Cables included Better kits bundle HDMI/DP + USB cables and a controller — saves ~$30 vs. buying separately. 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is a KVM switch and do I need one?
 A KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) switch lets two or more computers share one set of peripherals — and usually one monitor — so you press a button instead of unplugging cables. You need one if you run a work laptop and a personal or gaming PC at the same desk and want a single keyboard, mouse, and screen for both. If you only ever use one machine at a time and never switch, you do not need one.
 Can a KVM switch use one monitor for two computers?
 Yes — that is the main job of a video KVM. An HDMI KVM like the UGREEN 4K@60Hz ($70) takes the HDMI output of both computers and sends whichever you select to a single monitor, along with your keyboard and mouse. If your monitor has two video inputs of its own, you can skip the video KVM entirely and use a cheaper peripheral-only switch (~$40) instead.
 Do I need a KVM switch if my monitor already has two inputs?
 Not a full video KVM — you only need a peripheral switch. If your monitor has, say, an HDMI and a DisplayPort input, plug one computer into each, switch the monitor input with its own button, and use a $40 USB sharing switch (like the UGREEN USB 3.0 box) to move your keyboard, mouse, and dock between the two. That is the cheapest correct setup for a lot of people.
 Will a KVM switch support 4K and high refresh rates?
 It depends on the video standard. HDMI KVMs like the UGREEN ($70) handle 4K@60Hz and up to 1080p@240Hz — fine for office work and mainstream gaming. For 4K at 144Hz you need a DisplayPort 1.4 KVM such as the TESmart ($160), which also passes G-Sync/FreeSync VRR. Check that the KVM's rated resolution and refresh match your monitor, not just its highest headline number.
 Can a KVM switch charge my laptop?
 Only USB-C models with Power Delivery. A USB-C KVM dock like the Cable Matters ($200) sends video, USB peripherals, and up to 100W of charging down one cable to each laptop, so docking replaces a charger and a dongle at once. Standard HDMI and DisplayPort KVMs do not carry power — they only switch video and USB.
 Does a KVM switch work with both Mac and Windows?
 Yes. Every pick here is plug-and-play with no drivers on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and the USB-C dock is Thunderbolt 4 compatible so it works across a MacBook and a Windows laptop. The one thing to check is your keyboard: some Mac-specific keys behave differently when the same keyboard is switched to a Windows machine, but typing and the mouse work normally on both.

 What to Look for in a KVM Switch for Two Laptops
 Key buying criteria so you get the right fit the first time.
 01 Verify EDID emulation is included, regardless of price
 EDID (Extended Display Identification Data) is the information a monitor sends to a connected computer describing its supported resolutions and refresh rates, and a KVM switch without EDID emulation can cause a real, recurring annoyance: when you switch away from a computer, that computer loses its connection to the monitor's EDID data, and some graphics drivers respond by dropping to a default low resolution or losing the display arrangement entirely until you manually reconfigure it after switching back.
 A switch with proper EDID emulation stores and continuously presents the monitor's display information to every connected computer regardless of which one is actively selected, so switching back and forth doesn't repeatedly trigger resolution resets or display rearrangement.
 This feature isn't reliably tied to price, a budget switch can include it while a similarly priced competitor omits it, so check the listing or current buyer reviews specifically for EDID emulation rather than assuming it based on price alone.
 02 Match USB peripheral support to what you actually plug in, not just keyboard and mouse
 0 or higher) vary significantly beyond that baseline, and this matters concretely if you also want to switch a USB webcam, external drive, audio interface, or other peripheral along with the computer selection rather than leaving it permanently connected to one machine.
 0 ports can handle a webcam or external drive at full speed as part of the same switching action.
 Count your actual USB peripherals beyond keyboard and mouse, and check both the port count and the stated USB generation against what those specific peripherals need to function at full speed.
 03 Check whether switching happens via hotkey, a physical button, or both, and whether that matches your workflow
 KVM switches offer switching through a physical button on the device itself, a keyboard hotkey combination (commonly a specific key pressed a set number of times), or both, and this is a genuine day-to-day usability factor rather than a minor detail, since a physical button requires reaching across or behind your desk setup every time you switch, while hotkey switching lets you change computers without moving your hands from the keyboard at all.
 This matters more the more frequently you actually switch between computers during a session, someone switching once or twice a day may not care, while someone switching dozens of times while referencing one machine and working on another benefits meaningfully from hotkey support.
 Check whether hotkey switching is explicitly supported and confirm the specific key combination works with your operating system, since some hotkey implementations have compatibility quirks on certain OS versions.
 04 Confirm audio switching is included if you need it, since many KVM switches handle video and USB but not audio
 A significant number of KVM switches route video and USB peripherals between computers but do not switch audio output at all, meaning your speakers or headphones stay connected to whichever computer they were originally plugged into regardless of which computer is currently selected for video and keyboard control, a confusing experience if you're not expecting it.
 This is a distinct, separately-implemented feature, not something that comes automatically bundled with video and USB switching, so a switch's audio support (or lack of it) needs to be checked explicitly rather than assumed.
 If you regularly use audio output and want it to follow the same switching action as your monitor and keyboard, check the listing specifically for stated audio switching support rather than assuming any KVM switch handles this by default.
 05 Check physical port placement and cable routing, since a technically capable switch can still be annoying to use daily
 Beyond core specs like resolution support and port count, the physical layout of a KVM switch's ports on its housing meaningfully affects how pleasant it is to actually live with on a desk: ports crammed close together can make thick HDMI or USB-C cables difficult to seat fully, and ports facing an awkward direction relative to how the switch sits on or under your desk can turn routine cable management into a recurring frustration that a spec sheet never reveals.
 This is exactly the kind of detail that only shows up in real photos of the actual unit or in buyer reviews mentioning cable fit and port spacing, not in the resolution and port-count specs that dominate most listings.
 Look at actual product photos showing port placement and spacing before buying, and check reviews specifically for mentions of cable clearance issues if you're using thicker high-speed cables.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Does a USB-C KVM switch work the same with both my laptops?
 Only if both laptops' USB-C ports support video output, verify this for both devices before assuming symmetric switching performance.
 Will a KVM switch charge both my laptops at once?
 Usually not, power delivery typically only charges one connected device at a time, plan to keep both laptop power adapters in use.
 Should I use HDMI instead of USB-C for a two-laptop KVM switch?
 If either laptop's USB-C video support is uncertain, HDMI avoids that compatibility question entirely.
 Do I need a dual-monitor switch for two laptops?
 Only if you want a full workspace switch, a single-monitor switch is simpler and sufficient for many two-laptop workflows.
